My impression is that as you get older, you have a harder time coming back from traumas. There can be a stairstep effect to the aging process. unfortunately, recuperation when you're older is problematic (I know, I'm a couple years older than Hillary). Once you have major trauma, it IS harder to come back, but you can. Main thing is to emphasize health, don't neglect eating well and exercising properly, and to take care of issues when they crop up. I'm also not a fan of doctors, since my Dad and Mom wound up with a dozen or more prescriptions the docs wanted them to take all the time. My ex-wife argued that these prescriptions kept them alive, but I'm not so sure. One big thing is vaccinations. Jack LaLanne died of pneumonia at 95, after leading a very active life. It may have been "his time," but I know that he was opposed to medicine (I'm not, just believe in moderation), and possibly had not received his pneumonia vaccine. So at 71, I still keep lifting weights and riding my bike, hiking from time to time, and getting fresh air. So I use bicycles as my main mode of transportation. I bike to work, school, groceries and anything else nearby. One of my bikes got stolen a long time after when I left it outside my house by mistake, so after that, I started to lock my bike with two u-locks. I cut down to one lock after switching from panniers to a backpack for my commute. That turned out to be a costly mistake a few days ago. I clocked out of work a few nights ago and walked back to my bike only to find that it was lying on the ground with the front wheel missing. The thief had pried at my (Kryptonite) u-lock and mangled it up so much that it wouldn't open with a key. The rear wheel was locked up by this lock, so he took off with my front wheel instead. I got another cyclist to look around and he said he saw a homeless guy riding off with it.

So now here's my dilemma: I ride largely so I won't have to spend money on a car. But everyone who cycles around here has at least one theft story. One guy I asked even told me that he locked his bike frame up and came back to see the seatpost and both wheels taken, and pretty much only the bike frame left. Since I live in a high crime area, it's an absolute certainty that this is not the last time it's attempted against me.

I know all of the basic easy bike locking methods. I'm going to use at least two u-locks and keep the bikes locked in well watched areas. But what else can be done?

I've been so inconvenienced by this already that I'm trying to find out if I can get the local law enforcement, college or cycling groups to start a bait-bike program. The logical solution seems to be to actually track down the thieves for deterrence, but for catching thieves, there don't seem to be many (legal) options.
Rampant bike theft in my area / how to deal with it

The police will not help you ever. It is non violent, and low monetary value( they don't know about bikes that cost more then at Wal-Mart).

1) Get a New York proof lock that can't be cut. Kryptonite is NOT New York proof. They are breakable.

2) Insure your bike

3) Don't use an expensive bike.

It's not if, it's when.

Needlestack is correct. If your bike is out of sight, it's at risk for theft no matter what type of locking system you use. One of the main advantages of a folding bike is that it comes inside with you. I own one myself and I can't see why any serious cyclist wouldn't also own at least one folder.

Even a used brompton is an expensive investment though. Thankfully there are other options. There are a great deal of more affordable quality folding bikes out there to choose from. Two popular alternatives are tern and dahon. There's also the xootr swift, but it doesn't fold down as small as other folders. There are some brompton clones out there as well like flamingo or birdie. Last but certainly not least, there's bike friday, which is back on the pricier side but has a very well earned reputation.

There's also innumerable cheaper and lesser known alternatives which I'd personally stay away from. You don't want to be too cheap when it comes to a folding bike because quality is much more critical. Avoid the cheap ones.

Carrying a couple of panniers on a folder is totally doable. I can do so on mine. Lots of models come with a rack. Just do your homework before you buy and you should be set to go. That's the key takeaway: do your research. If you do, you'll end up with a bike that won't disappoint.

You'll probably want something that can at least fit inside a shopping cart, which means having 20" wheels at the largest, although you can find 26" wheel folders if that's your thing, but I honestly think 20" is the magic size when it comes to folders.
